name: Janamejaya
role: Kuru king who heard the Mahabharata and held the snake sacrifice
summary: Janamejaya is the Kuru king, son of Parikshit, to whom the Mahabharata is first recited, and who holds the great snake sacrifice that the sage Astika halts.
about: In the Mahabharata, Janamejaya is the son of Parikshit and Madravati, grandson of Abhimanyu and great-grandson of Arjuna. The epic says he succeeded his father on the Kuru throne. The text frames its own telling around him: Vaishampayana, a pupil of Vyasa, recites the story to him. After the Naga king Takshaka caused Parikshit's death, the epic says Janamejaya held a sarpa satra, a sacrifice meant to destroy the serpents, until the young sage Astika persuaded him to stop. Earlier Vedic works such as the Aitareya and Shatapatha Brahmanas also mention a king of this name as a conqueror who performed a horse sacrifice. Historians debate how these Vedic and epic figures relate.
kidSummary: Janamejaya is a king in the Mahabharata who is the very first to hear its whole story. When his father is lost to a snake, he starts a huge sacrifice to stop the serpents, but a wise boy named Astika asks him to stop, and he listens.

story.title: A royal family
story.text: Janamejaya is the son of King Parikshit, and the great-grandson of Arjuna. When his father passes away, he becomes the king of the Kurus.

story.title: The sad news
story.text: He learns that his father died because of a snake, Takshaka, the Naga king. Janamejaya is full of grief and starts planning something big.

story.title: The snake sacrifice
story.text: He begins a sarpa satra, a great sacrifice that pulls snakes toward the fire. Many snakes come to it, and Takshaka also is in danger.

story.title: A boy speaks up
story.text: A young sage named Astika, whose mother belongs to the snake family, asks the king for a favour. Janamejaya listens and ends the sacrifice.

story.title: The great story
story.text: The story of his ancestors, the Mahabharata, is told to him by Vaishampayana, a pupil of Vyasa.

teaches: Listening can turn anger into kindness
Wisdom can come from the young

quiz.why: He is the son of Parikshit.

quiz.q: Which sage persuaded him to stop the snake sacrifice?
quiz.why: The young Astika asked him to stop.

quiz.q: Who was the Naga king connected to his father's death?
quiz.why: Takshaka carried out the curse in the epic.

quiz.q: Which festival is linked to the end of the snake sacrifice?
quiz.why: Tradition links Naga Panchami to the day Astika saved the snakes.

quiz.q: Who first recited the Mahabharata to him?

facts.text: The Mahabharata names Vaishampayana, Vyasa's pupil, as the first to recite the epic, and Janamejaya as the listener.
Takshaka, in the epic, reached Parikshit by hiding as a worm in a fruit. Parikshit had been sheltered in a guarded mansion on one pillar.
Naga Panchami, on the fifth lunar day of Shravana, is linked by tradition to Astika's saving of the snakes.
A pond called Parikshit Kund in Mainpuri district is said to mark the sacrifice pit. A local legend says snakes there stay harmless.
Four copper-plate land grants once claimed to be from his reign were shown by scholars to be forgeries.
At a long sacrifice at Kurukshetra, Janamejaya's brothers beat the dog son of Sarama. When they stayed silent, she cursed that misfortune would strike him when he least expected it.
The Vayu and Matsya Puranas speak of a quarrel with Vaishampayana, after which he may have given up the throne to his son Shatanika. Another list names his grandson Ashvamedhadatha as his successor.
Historians credit Janamejaya and his father Parikshit with making the Kuru realm the leading power of northern India, collecting Vedic hymns and shaping the srauta rituals.
The sage Uttanka came to Janamejaya, who had just returned victorious from Takshashila, and told him that Takshaka had killed his father. He urged the king to hold a snake sacrifice in revenge.
At the snake sacrifice, Takshaka hid with Indra, coiled round his seat. The priests chanted harder, and the pull dragged Indra himself, with his throne, toward the sacrificial fire.
The young sage Astika who halted the sacrifice was the son of a Brahmin, Jaratkaru, and of Manasa, a Naga woman. That is why he could plead for the snakes.
Astika was offered a boon, and the king never refused a boon to a Brahmin. So Janamejaya stopped the sacrifice, even though the priests protested.
In the Naga Panchami telling, the frightened gods asked the snake goddess Manasa for help. She sent her son Astika, and afterwards Indra himself worshipped her.
The Panchavimsha Brahmana names a Janamejaya as a priest at a snake sacrifice, but scholars Macdonell and Keith thought he was a different man from the Kuru king.
The Aitareya Brahmana says that at one sacrifice he did not use the Kashyapas as priests but the Bhutaviras. He later brought the Asitamriga family of Kashyapas back.
The Shatapatha Brahmana says he and three brothers performed a horse sacrifice to cleanse themselves of sin, led by the priest Indrota Daivapa Shaunaka.
Historian H. C. Raychaudhuri dates his father Parikshit to about the ninth century BCE. Michael Witzel links the Pariksit dynasty to Black and Red Ware pottery dated about 1180 BCE.
Versions differ on Takshaka's fate: one telling has him dragged toward the fire with Indra, while the Takshaka article says Janamejaya's men traced him and brought him as a prisoner.
The epic names his mother as Madravati and gives him three brothers, Shrutasena, Ugrasena and Bhimasena.
The Gopatha Brahmana tells an anecdote about Janamejaya and two ganders, which the Wikipedia article calls absurd.
